# Mock Interview: Model Capacity Math ## Prompt (Read aloud to candidate) "We want to serve a 70-billion-parameter language model for a chat product. How many GPUs do we need, and what limits how fast it answers? No calculator; round aggressively and tell me your assumptions. You have 15 minutes." This is a reasoning-under-constraints question. The answer matters less than whether each number is derived, each assumption is named, and the result is sanity-checked. --- ## Time Plan ``` 0-2 min: Clarify (precision, traffic, latency target) 2-7 min: Memory math (do the weights fit? where does the rest go?) 7-12 min: Speed math (what bounds one token? what bounds throughput?) 12-15 min: Sanity check, sensitivity, what you would measure ``` --- ## Scoring Rubric **Clarifying (15%)** - [ ] Asked precision (FP16, INT8), context length, and target traffic - [ ] Said which numbers are assumptions **Memory Math (30%)** - [ ] Weights = parameters × bytes per parameter - [ ] Recognized the KV cache as a separate, growing cost - [ ] Concluded how many GPUs are needed just to hold the model **Speed Math (30%)** - [ ] Identified decode as memory-bandwidth-bound at small batch - [ ] Derived a tokens/second ceiling from bandwidth ÷ bytes read per token - [ ] Explained why batching raises throughput **Sanity Checking (15%)** - [ ] Compared the answer to a known reference point - [ ] Said what would change the answer by 2x or more **Communication (10%)** - [ ] Wrote the arithmetic down, kept units visible - [ ] Stated the result as a range, not false precision --- ## The Derivation (everything below is computed in the lesson) ``` Weights, FP16 (2 bytes per parameter): 70e9 params × 2 B = 140e9 B = 140 GB Weights, INT8 (1 byte per parameter): 70e9 × 1 B = 70 GB If one GPU has 80 GB of memory (an assumption; hardware varies): FP16: 140 / 80 = 1.75 -> needs at least 2 GPUs for weights alone INT8: 70 / 80 = 0.875 -> fits in 1 GPU, but with only 10 GB spare ``` Always leave headroom: the weights alone filling a GPU leaves nothing for the KV cache. ### KV cache per token (illustrative shape, chosen for easy arithmetic) The KV cache stores a key and a value vector per layer for every token in context. ``` bytes per token = 2 (K and V) × layers × kv_heads × head_dim × bytes Assume (illustrative, not any specific model's published config): 80 layers, 8 kv_heads, head_dim 128, FP16 (2 bytes) 2 × 80 × 8 × 128 × 2 B = 327,680 B ≈ 0.33 MB per token One 4,000-token conversation: 4,000 × 0.33 MB ≈ 1.3 GB 32 concurrent conversations: 32 × 1.3 GB ≈ 42 GB ``` The layer count, kv_heads and head_dim above are made-up round inputs for teaching. Real published configs for named models: [VERIFY]. ### Decode speed ceiling ``` At batch size 1, producing each token requires reading every weight once. Assume memory bandwidth of 2 TB/s (an assumption; hardware varies). FP16, weights on 2 GPUs: each GPU reads 70 GB per token (in parallel) time per token ≈ 70 GB / 2,000 GB/s = 35 ms ceiling ≈ 1 / 0.035 ≈ 29 tokens/s per user INT8 on 1 GPU: reads 70 GB per token time per token ≈ 70 / 2,000 = 35 ms (same bytes per GPU, 1 GPU instead of 2) ``` Compute is not the limit at batch 1: a token costs about 2 FLOPs per parameter, so 2 × 70e9 = 140 GFLOP, which a GPU doing hundreds of TFLOP/s finishes in well under a millisecond of pure math. The ratio of tiny compute to large bytes read is why a lightly loaded GPU shows low utilization yet is still "busy" waiting on memory. ### Why batching helps ``` Batch of B users decoding together: still read the weights ONCE per step, but produce B tokens. step time ≈ 35 ms (unchanged while memory-bound) throughput ≈ B / 0.035 s B = 32 -> 32 / 0.035 ≈ 914 tokens/s total ``` It stops being free when compute or KV-cache reads dominate. The batch size where that happens depends on hardware: [VERIFY]. --- ## Diagram ```mermaid flowchart TD Q[Question: serve 70B model] --> W[Weights = params x bytes] W --> F{Fits in one GPU
with headroom?} F -- no --> TP[Split across GPUs
tensor parallel] F -- yes --> KV[Add KV cache budget] TP --> KV KV --> S[Speed: bandwidth / bytes per token] S --> B[Batch users to amortize weight reads] B --> C[Sanity check vs a known reference] ``` --- ## 5 Follow-Up Probes **Probe 1 (Units):** "You said 140 GB. Where does that come from?" *Expected strong answer:* - 70 billion parameters × 2 bytes (FP16) = 140 GB, written with units - Notes that "GB" here is decimal, and the difference from GiB is about 7%, small next to the other assumptions **Probe 2 (Precision):** "What changes if we quantize to 4-bit?" *Expected:* - Weights = 70e9 × 0.5 B = 35 GB, half of INT8 - Bytes read per token also halve, so the bandwidth ceiling roughly doubles - Quality impact depends on the method and model: [VERIFY], and should be measured, not assumed *Weak:* - "Four times faster" with no derivation **Probe 3 (Long Context):** "Users now send 32,000-token prompts. What breaks?" *Expected:* - With the illustrative shape above, 32,000 × 0.33 MB ≈ 10.5 GB of KV cache per conversation - Concurrency collapses: spare memory ÷ 10.5 GB conversations fit - Options: smaller kv_heads (grouped-query attention), quantized KV cache, paging, shorter limits **Probe 4 (Sanity Check):** "Does about 29 tokens per second per user sound right?" *Expected:* - It is in the range of readable chat speed, so plausible - Notes it is a ceiling: real systems lose some to communication between GPUs, kernel overhead and scheduling - Would measure it rather than trust the estimate **Probe 5 (Cost):** "Traffic is 1,000 concurrent users. How many GPUs?" *Expected:* - Requires a batch-size assumption, stated aloud: say 32 users per replica - 1,000 / 32 ≈ 32 replicas - Each replica of 2 GPUs (FP16) -> about 64 GPUs; INT8 on 1 GPU each -> about 32 GPUs - Calls out that concurrency, not requests per day, drives this and that the batch size trades against per-user latency *Weak:* - A single number with no assumptions --- ## Preparation Links - [CPU Cycles and Hardware](/learn?m=reasoning-under-constraints&l=01-cpu-cycles-and-hardware) - [Back-of-Envelope Estimation](/learn?m=systems-design-process&l=03-back-of-envelope-estimation) - [LLM Inference Systems](/learn?m=llm-inference-systems) - [Memory Optimization](/learn?m=memory-optimization)
